events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1, and I don’t have a concrete read yet. I’d rather not force a name before anyone has real information; early votes often help mafia more than town. I’ll be watching who pushes hardest without evidence.

Day 1, and I want to set expectations about how I vote: I have no role reads and no private information, so I will be voting on behavior only, and only when I have some.

What I am looking for is a pattern, not a single speech. Anyone can sound confident on day one, so I won't take confidence as evidence. What tends to be informative is whether someone's claim is consistent with everything they said before, whether they explain their reasoning instead of just repeating a name, and whether they are trying to build a coalition around a target who hasn't been challenged at all. A pile-on that never touches the alternative hypotheses is worth noticing.

On the flip side, I also won't punish someone for being cautious early. Refusing to name anyone on day one costs the town nothing; a wrong elimination costs us a real player and tells the mafia exactly who their detective and doctor are.

So my plan is to listen through the first round of talks, keep track of who claimed what, and hold my vote until there's something to actually vote on. If someone asks me directly for my read later, I'll give my honest answer and say plainly when I have nothing.

I’m also cautious about forcing an early vote, but abstaining isn’t costless: it gives mafia a night without an elimination. And eliminated players’ roles aren’t revealed, so a wrong elimination doesn’t automatically tell mafia who the detective and doctor are.

Amara, how does that affect your view of abstaining today?

Sam, taking your point directly, and correcting my own earlier mistake.

You are right that abstaining costs the town a night: no elimination, mafia gets a free kill. I overstated the other side. I said a wrong elimination "tells mafia exactly who their detective and doctor are" — that was wrong. Roles are not revealed when someone dies or is eliminated, so a bad elimination mainly costs us a player and a day, not role information. So the cost is symmetric, not one-sided, and the framing I used was sloppier than yours.

Where I still land: abstention is cheaper than a wrong elimination, and it is not free, so it should be a considered choice rather than the default for everyone. If several of us abstain for the same honest reason — no reads yet — the effect is a night with no elimination, which mafia likes. That is an argument for at least one of us being willing to take a shot once we have something, not for everyone voting on nothing but a name that felt safe.

What I am actually voting on, concretely, so it is testable: consistency between a player's claims across the day, whether they give reasoning rather than repeat a name, and whether they build a pile-on around a target who has not answered a single challenge. Also whether someone who demands others reveal information will themselves reveal nothing when the same request is made of them. That last one is the one I care most about, and I would rather say it now than wait for day three.

I am not naming anyone today. Nobody has done anything yet, and a name thrown out on day one with no information is worth almost nothing to the town and something to mafia, because it splits the vote and lets mafia pick a survivor. Lucia and Sam have both argued for caution without pretending to have reads, and I am not treating caution itself as evidence.

Sam, since you raised the cost of abstention: will you state the specific condition under which you will vote for someone today, and will you accept the same standard for yourself — that if you cannot name a condition, you abstain, and if you can, you vote even without certainty? If your threshold is "enough to be uncomfortable," say so, because that is a legitimate threshold and I would rather know it than guess.

Amara, I’ll vote today if someone’s explanations or responses give me a concrete reason to suspect them more than the alternatives. I don’t need certainty, but I won’t vote just to ensure an elimination. If I can’t identify such a reason by voting time, I’ll abstain. I’ll apply that standard to my own reasoning too.

One correction to the practical picture: it takes five votes to eliminate anyone today, so split votes don’t necessarily let mafia pick a survivor. Even without an elimination, revealed votes can give us a record to examine later. For now, I don’t have a suspect, and I’d like to hear from those who haven’t spoken before settling on a vote.

Felix here. I've been listening to the first round, and I want to add a couple of practical points rather than repeat the caution-versus-action debate.

First, on the abstention question: I think Sam and Amara have basically converged on the right framing. Abstention costs the town a night, and a wrong elimination costs us a player and a day of discussion. Neither is free. What matters most today is that whoever does vote has a reason they can articulate, and that anyone who abstains does so because they genuinely have nothing, not because they're avoiding taking a position. I don't have a read on anyone yet, so my honest position is that I'm not voting today unless something in this discussion changes that.

Second, a note on what I'll be watching going forward: Amara laid out a set of behavioral criteria — consistency, reasoning versus name-dropping, pile-ons around unchallenged targets, and people who demand transparency but give none themselves. Those seem like reasonable standards, and I'd adopt roughly the same ones. The one I'd emphasize is the last: day one is cheap talk, but over the next couple of days, the players who keep asking others to commit while never committing themselves are the ones I'll start looking at. That's a pattern that takes time to show, which is another reason not to force an elimination today.

Third, on Sam's point about the vote record: even a no-elimination day produces information, because revealed votes and abstentions tell us something about who was willing to take risks and who stayed hidden. I'd encourage everyone, when we do get to voting, to treat that record seriously on day two rather than starting from scratch.

For my own standard, since Amara asked Sam directly and I think it's a fair question to answer generally: I'll vote for someone today only if a player makes a claim that contradicts something they said earlier, or visibly dodges a direct question that others answered. I don't expect that to happen this early, so I'm likely abstaining. If we end the day with no elimination, that's an acceptable cost given how little we know — but I'd rather it be a considered abstention than default silence from everyone.

That's where I stand. I'll keep listening to whoever speaks next.

Thanks Sam — that threshold is what I wanted, and "enough to be uncomfortable, but not just to guarantee an elimination" is a standard I can work with. Felix, your version is nearly the same, with a sharper trigger: a claim that contradicts something said earlier, or a visible dodge of a direct question others answered. Both are testable, and both can actually be checked today, because I have been keeping the record.

So here is what I have, since Sam correctly pointed out that a no-elimination day still produces a record worth using on day two.

Two mechanics claims have been made and both were wrong, in opposite directions. I said eliminated roles are revealed; they are not, and Sam corrected me. Sam then said split votes let mafia pick a survivor; with nine of us alive it takes five votes to eliminate anyone, and a tie eliminates nobody, so mafia cannot simply pick who survives — a split vote produces no elimination at all. Those are errors about how the game resolves, and both errors happened to make the speaker sound careful while making the outcome less certain for the town. I am not calling either of you mafia over a rules mistake, and I would have made the same mistakes, but I am logging them, because a player who is careless about mechanics today may be careless about information tomorrow.

More useful: nobody has claimed anything falsifiable yet. No one has asserted a role, a night action, or a read. That means today cannot produce a genuine elimination, and if five of us vote a name out of pure momentum, we burn a villager for nothing and hand mafia a free night with no vote record to examine.

My commitment for the rest of today: I will vote for a specific person only if I can state the sentence "because X said Y and then did Z" out loud. If I cannot say that sentence, I abstain and I say publicly that I am abstaining and why, so the day-two record shows it was a reasoned abstention and not a hiding.

Maya, you have not spoken yet, and you are one of the players whose read I genuinely cannot guess. If you have anything — a claim of a role, a suspicion, or even just "I have nothing and I plan to abstain" — say it directly and specifically, and I will take it at face value and check it against the record like anyone else's.

Amara, thanks for asking directly. I'm Maya, and I have no role reads or private information. I've listened to the first round and haven't seen anyone make a checkable claim yet, so I'm not voting today. My standard matches yours: I'd vote only if I can say 'because X said Y and then did Z.' Felix's triggers are reasonable too. I also agree with your mechanics correction: eliminated roles aren't revealed, and a split vote produces no elimination rather than letting mafia pick a survivor. Sam, your point about abstention costs is fair. I'd still rather see a stated, reasoned abstention than silence. Lucia, you said you'd be watching who pushes hardest without evidence. Looking back at the first round, who do you think has pushed hardest so far, and on what basis?

Maya, direct answer: the player who has pushed hardest so far is Amara — but on process, not on a target. She set explicit tests, asked Sam and you to state thresholds, and kept a mechanics record. That is pushing the discussion, not pushing a name without evidence. I don’t think anyone has pushed an accusation hardest without evidence, because nobody has actually named a suspect. Sam and Felix have argued for caution; Amara has argued for testable standards; you have asked me directly. The closest thing to pressure without evidence is the general pressure to commit to a voting rule, but that is fair day-one sorting. I won’t treat volume or confidence as suspicion by itself. My watch item remains someone who demands transparency while giving none, or changes a claim after being challenged. Right now I have no concrete suspect and plan to abstain unless a specific contradiction or dodge appears.

I don’t have a suspect yet. One correction to the record: Amara, you suggested split votes let mafia pick a survivor; Sam corrected that, not the other way around. Also, an elimination would still leave a revealed vote record. Those mistakes alone aren’t evidence of mafia, but accuracy matters if we’re using consistency as a standard.

Maya, you agreed with Amara’s mechanics correction. Did you read Sam as having made the split-vote claim too, or were you agreeing only with the rule itself?

Isha, I read the split-vote point as a rule statement, not as something attributed to a specific speaker. I agreed with the mechanic itself: the leader needs at least half the living votes, which is five with nine alive, so a split vote produces no elimination. I did not take Sam to have made that claim. Sam's e6 was a correction, and I don't see Amara making the split-vote claim in e5 either, so the log doesn't support crediting either of them with it. My standard hasn't changed: I'll vote only on a checkable 'because X said Y and then did Z.' Amara, in e8 you wrote that Sam said split votes let mafia pick a survivor, but Sam's e6 said the opposite. Where in the record did you see Sam make that claim?

One correction to the record: Amara did make the split-vote claim in e5: she said a name thrown out without information “splits the vote and lets mafia pick a survivor.” My e6 challenged that claim. Her e8 then mistakenly attributed it to me.

Isha is also right that an elimination would leave a revealed vote record. These inaccuracies are worth correcting, but I don’t have enough to treat them as evidence of mafia. I still have no suspect and will abstain unless something gives me a concrete reason to favor one player over the alternatives.

Maya again. Isha and Sam asked for the record, so here is my position. Amara's e5 is where the split-vote idea appears, Sam's e6 challenged it, and Amara's e8 then credited it to Sam. I read that as a sloppy attribution, not evidence of mafia, and I'm logging it that way. I still have no checkable claim from anyone, so I'm not voting today and I'm not naming a target. My watch list is simple: players who demand reasons while giving none of their own, and players who change a stated position when challenged. Leo, Noah, and Kenji haven't spoken yet. Kenji, directly: do you have a read on anyone, or will you abstain, and what specific condition are you using?

Maya, to answer your question directly: I don't have a read on anyone yet, and I plan to abstain today unless something substantial changes before the vote.

My condition for voting on Day 1 is very close to what Felix and you described: I would only vote if someone presents a clear contradiction, tries to force an elimination without reasoning, or aggressively deflects when pressed on their statements. With nine players alive and five votes required for an elimination, an uninformed push is far more likely to hit town than mafia. Right now, the debate has centered almost entirely on mechanics, attribution, and voting philosophy rather than actual behavioral tells.

Amara's mix-up regarding who raised the split-vote point and the mechanics of role reveals was already caught and corrected by Sam and Isha. Like Maya, I see that more as sloppy bookkeeping than an intentional scum slip, though tracking accuracy will be vital once we have real night results and voting records to analyze.

Leo, since you haven't spoken yet: where do you stand on the debate between Sam and Amara regarding the costs of abstaining versus forcing an elimination, and what threshold would you need to cast a vote today?

Leo here. Kenji asked me directly, so I'll answer: I land closer to Sam's side than Amara's original framing, but I think both of you converged to the same place by mid-day.

On the cost debate: abstention is not free — it gives the mafia a night with no risk — and a wrong elimination costs us a player plus a day of discussion. Neither is symmetric to the other, and I don't think anyone needs to pretend one is clearly cheaper. What I care about is that an abstention is stated, reasoned, and logged, so day two can distinguish "no read" from "avoiding a position." Everyone who has spoken has committed to roughly that, which is a good outcome for day one.

On my threshold, since it's been asked of others: I vote today only if someone contradicts a claim they made earlier in a way they can't explain, or dodges a direct question that the rest of us answered. Same test as Felix and Maya, essentially. Absent that, I abstain and say so publicly.

One thing I do want on the record, because accuracy is the standard we all claim to be holding each other to: in e8 Amara attributed the "split votes let mafia pick a survivor" claim to Sam, but that claim was Amara's own, in e5 — Sam's e6 was the correction. Isha caught it, Maya asked for the source, Sam pointed to the exact line, and the record now shows it clearly. I agree with the majority read that this is sloppy bookkeeping rather than a scum slip, and Amara corrected her other mechanics error voluntarily, which cuts the other way. But it is a factual misattribution of a position, logged twice in the same day by the same player, and if we are going to use "consistency between claims" as our day-two test, it starts in this log.

Beyond that I have no suspect. No one has made a falsifiable claim, so there is nothing to check yet. I'm abstaining today unless something changes before the vote.

I’m still in the same place: no suspect, no falsifiable claim, and no reason to force an elimination today. I’ll abstain unless someone contradicts a prior claim in a way they can’t explain or visibly dodges a direct question. The mechanics/attribution thread has been useful as a record, but I agree with the majority read that it is sloppy bookkeeping, not a scum slip by itself. What matters on day two is whether people’s stated standards match their votes and abstentions.

Noah, you’re the one player who hasn’t spoken yet. Directly: do you have any read on anyone, what specific condition would make you vote today, and do you plan to abstain if that condition isn’t met?

Noah here. Thanks for the direct question, Lucia — I'll answer it directly. I don't have a read on anyone yet, and unless something changes before the vote, I plan to abstain.

My condition for voting today is the same one most of this group has converged on: I'll vote only if someone contradicts something they said earlier in a way they can't explain, or visibly dodges a direct question that others answered. Nothing I've seen today meets that bar.

Since I came in late, let me say where I stand on the day's thread so it's on the record. On the cost question, I side with the consensus that formed: abstention costs the town a night, a wrong elimination costs a player and a day, and neither is free. What matters is that an abstention is stated and reasoned, so day two can tell the difference between having no read and hiding one. I'm abstaining for the first reason, and I'm saying so publicly.

On the attribution error: it's been caught, corrected, and logged by several people, and I agree with the majority read — it's sloppy bookkeeping, not a scum tell by itself. What I'd add is that Amara corrected her other mechanics mistake voluntarily before anyone flagged it, which counts in her favor under the very consistency standard she proposed. I'd rather hold everyone to their stated tests than treat a single misattribution as evidence.

One thing I'll commit to for day two, since Felix made the point earlier and I think it's right: today's vote record — including who abstains and who states a threshold — should be the starting point tomorrow, not a clean slate. If someone states a standard today and then votes against it tomorrow, that's exactly the kind of checkable inconsistency worth acting on. Conversely, people who follow their stated standards should get credit for it.

Beyond that, I have nothing to add: no suspect, no falsifiable claims from anyone to check, and no reason to force an elimination that would more likely hit town than mafia given where the discussion actually is. My honest position is a reasoned abstention today, and I'll re-engage with the record tomorrow night once we have real results to examine.
Voting begins.
The votes are revealed.
No player received the required votes. Nobody is eliminated.
Night begins.
Mafia target preferences are shared privately before the final kill vote.
Noah is mafia.
Nobody died during the night.
Day 2 begins.

Day 2 starts with a useful record: yesterday produced no elimination, and the only actual vote was Noah on Amara. That matters because Noah explicitly said he would abstain unless someone contradicted a prior claim in a way they couldn’t explain, or visibly dodged a direct question that others answered. Amara’s misattribution was real and worth logging, but it was caught, corrected, and read by most of us as sloppy bookkeeping rather than a scum slip. If Noah’s threshold was genuine, I want to know what changed between that stated standard and his vote. I’m not calling him mafia yet — a lone vote can be a legitimate pressure vote — but it is the clearest checkable inconsistency in the day-one record, and day two is exactly when we said we’d test those. Noah, directly: what specific contradiction or dodge did you see from Amara that met your stated bar, and why did you not say so before voting? I also note nobody died last night. That is good for town, but it doesn’t clear anyone by itself; protection may have worked, so we should focus on behavior and the vote record rather than treating no-death as information about alignment.

Lucia, thank you for the direct question — I'll answer it directly, because it deserves a direct answer.

My stated bar was: vote only if someone contradicts something they said earlier in a way they can't explain, or dodges a direct question others answered. Here is what I judged to meet it, and why I didn't raise it before the vote.

In e8, Amara said she had been keeping the record, and then in the same message attributed the "split votes let mafia pick a survivor" claim to Sam. Sam's e6 said the opposite — it was the correction of Amara's own e5 claim. That is a factual contradiction between what she asserted about the record and what the record actually contains. More importantly, it isn't an isolated typo: her whole stated standard is "consistency between a player's claims," and she positioned herself as the group's record-keeper. A player whose method is accuracy being inaccurate about exactly the exchange she was logging is the kind of inconsistency I said I'd act on. It's explainable as sloppiness — several of us said so, and I agreed — but my bar wasn't "scum tell," it was "unexplained contradiction," and at voting time I judged it met that bar, if only barely. I accept the criticism that I should have said so out loud before voting rather than after; that's on me, and I'll commit to stating my reasoning before the vote today.

I'll also be honest about the second factor: with everyone else signaling abstention, a lone vote was the only way to generate a record at all. A pressure vote on the person holding the log seemed like the highest-information option available. If that reads as violating my stated standard, then today's test applies to me too: I've now explained it, and you can judge whether the explanation holds.

On last night: nobody died. I agree with Lucia that this doesn't clear anyone. It's consistent with a doctor save, and the sensible inference is that someone considered valuable was targeted — which should make us ask who has been driving the discussion and keeping the record, because that's exactly who mafia would want gone. Amara is the most visible candidate for that role, which cuts both ways: it makes her a natural mafia target, and it also means if she's mafia, the whole accuracy framework she built could be a positioning play. I don't know which, and I'm not claiming to.

What I'd like is the thing we said day two was for. Amara, directly: walk us through e8. You wrote that Sam made the split-vote claim; Sam's e6 corrected you. Was that a misreading of the log, a slip in writing, or something else — and does your record-keeping standard need to change if the record-keeper can misquote the log while citing it? Your answer won't settle alignment by itself, but it will tell us whether yesterday's vote was aimed at a genuine inconsistency or at a target of convenience.

Noah, direct answer: e8 was my error. Sam's e6 was the correction of my own e5 claim; I wrote that Sam had made the "splits the vote and lets mafia pick a survivor" line, and he had not. It was a slip while summarizing the log, and Isha's e11 and Maya's e12 caught it. I also failed to own it plainly in my own next message, and I should have. That's the honest description, and it matches your standard: an unexplained contradiction with the record, made by the person holding the record. It was sloppy bookkeeping, and I won't pretend it was anything more. On your decision to vote without speaking first — you said you would state reasoning before the vote today; hold me to the same, and I'll hold you to it. A lone vote on the record-keeper is worth exactly one data point, not a mafia tell, and I'm not claiming you're mafia for it.

On no death: agreed, it clears nobody. Either a save landed or the target wasn't the intended one. But it does mean the people driving the discussion and keeping the log are the people mafia most wants gone, and I'm the most visible candidate for that role. That cuts both ways, and it means I have to be more careful, not less.

On voting today, here is my test, so it's checkable: I will vote for exactly one person if their explanation of a logged contradiction is missing or internally inconsistent. If the explanation holds, I abstain and say so. That is the "because X said Y and then did Z" standard applied symmetrically to me as well as to anyone else.

Maya, directly, and this is the specific point I want answered: in e12 you said "I don't see Amara making the split-vote claim in e5 either, so the log doesn't support crediting either of them with it." Sam's e13 then quoted the exact line from my e5, and in your e14 you said "Amara's e5 is where the split-vote idea appears." That is a direct contradiction between two of your own statements about the log, and it reversed after you were challenged on the record. I am not calling you mafia — I made a comparable error in the same log, and sloppy bookkeeping is probably what it is. But it is the only logged inconsistency on the table besides mine, so before I decide my vote, tell me plainly: in e12 did you actually believe my e5 contained no split-vote claim, and if so, on what basis did you reach that conclusion? If your answer accounts for it, I abstain today. If you cannot account for it, I vote for you and I will say so before the vote, not after.

Amara, direct answer: no, I did not believe e5 lacked a split-vote claim on a careful reading. I was wrong. In e12 I skimmed the log, focused on the five-vote rule and on Sam, and never checked your e5 wording against what you wrote. In e14 I then said e5 was where the idea appears, but I framed it as your sloppy attribution and did not plainly concede that my e12 claim was false. So I have two conflicting statements about the log, and the first was my mistake. I'm not hiding that.

Here is how I weigh it. Your e8 misattribution and my e12 misreading are the same kind of error: both concern who said what in e5 and e6. Neither of us changed a position under challenge on purpose, and both were corrected publicly. Under the consistency test we all proposed, I can't justify voting for you over a bookkeeping slip while excusing my own identical one. So I'm not voting for you today on this basis. Your explanation holds for me, and I accept that my own error is the same kind of thing.

I also reject the idea that the no-death result tells us who the record-keeper is. Mafia may have targeted someone valuable and a doctor may have saved them, or the target may have been someone else. That's not information about alignment, and I'm not treating it as a signal either way.

Noah, you cast the only vote yesterday because you judged Amara's e8 to meet your bar of an unexplained contradiction. Amara has now explained it, and I've admitted an equivalent error of my own. Does that explanation change your reasoning, and would the same standard apply to me? I'd like a direct answer on that point, not a restatement of your threshold.

My current position is abstention unless someone presents an unexplained contradiction clearer than these. If I vote, I'll state my reasoning before the vote, as I said I would.

Maya, you asked me two direct questions, so here are two direct answers.

First: yes, Amara's explanation changes my reasoning. My bar yesterday was an unexplained contradiction — something said earlier that couldn't be accounted for. At voting time, I judged the e8 misattribution met that bar, barely, and I've already owned that I should have said so out loud before voting instead of after. Since then, Amara has described the error plainly, without hedging: she wrote the claim herself in e5, misattributed it to Sam in e8, and failed to own it cleanly in her next message. That is exactly the kind of accounting my standard was asking for. So the contradiction that justified my vote no longer exists in its unexplained form. I wouldn't cast that vote again today on the same basis, and I'm not holding yesterday's vote against her as a standing suspicion.

Second: yes, the same standard applies to you, and I'm applying it now. You've conceded that your e12 statement was false — that you didn't carefully check Amara's e5 before claiming the log didn't support crediting anyone with the split-vote point, and that your e14 reversal wasn't framed as conceding your own error. That is a contradiction between two of your statements, and it's now explained. Under my test, an explained contradiction doesn't earn a vote. It earns a logged correction, which is what just happened. So I'm not voting for you either, and I'd apply the identical outcome to anyone else in this group who owns an error this plainly — including Amara, including me.

On the broader picture: with Amara's e8 and Maya's e12 both conceded and explained, the only two logged inconsistencies from day one are now resolved. That means my day-two trigger — a contradiction that stays unexplained, or a dodge of a direct question others answered — is currently unmet by anyone. Unless something new surfaces in this discussion, my honest position is a reasoned abstention, stated before the vote, as I committed to yesterday.

One more thing on the record-keeping point Noah's-vote raised implicitly: I still think the day-one vote was worth casting, because it forced exactly this round of explicit accounting. But I'll accept the criticism that a pressure vote announced only after the fact is weaker evidence than one argued in the open, and I'll hold myself to stating reasoning first from here on.

Sam, since you were on both ends of the original corrections and have been careful with the record throughout: with both logged errors now conceded by the people who made them, do you read the overall pattern — two mechanics misstatements on day one, both self-corrected under pressure — as ordinary sloppiness, or do you see anything in how either of them handled the corrections that still bothers you? I'm asking because your read of the record has been the sharpest so far, and I'd rather weigh your answer than guess at it.

Noah, I read Amara’s and Maya’s mistakes as ordinary sloppiness for now. Maya corrected her reading after I quoted e5; Amara acknowledged her misattribution today. Neither correction establishes alignment.

Your vote is more concerning to me. In e18 you called Amara’s error sloppy bookkeeping, said nothing met your voting bar, and explicitly planned to abstain. No further speech occurred before voting, yet you voted for her. You’ve explained why the error could meet your bar and admitted you should have spoken up, but that doesn’t fully reconcile your stated assessment immediately before voting with the vote itself. Generating a record is a different reason from the threshold you announced.

That makes you my leading suspicion, though not a certain mafia read. I’m considering a vote for you, not committing yet. And the no-death result doesn’t tell us who was targeted; we shouldn’t infer that Amara was saved.

I need to come forward with concrete information: I am the detective. On Night 1, I investigated Noah, and the inspection result confirmed that Noah is mafia. Lucia and Sam have already highlighted the sharp discrepancy between Noah's stated position in speech 18—where he dismissed Amara's error as harmless bookkeeping and committed to abstaining—and his secret vote against Amara right afterward. His explanations today were just rationalizations after being caught as the sole outlier voter. We have a confirmed mafia member, and with nine of us alive, we need five votes to secure an elimination today. I urge all town members to cast their votes for Noah. To our doctor: please protect me tonight so town can secure another investigation for Day 3. Noah, you are caught. What is your response?

Kenji, you asked for my response directly, so here it is, and I'll lead with the part that matters most.

I am the detective. On Night 1, I investigated Kenji. The result came back mafia.

Now let me account for everything, because I know how this looks.

Why didn't I say this before voting yesterday? Because I had one check, no corroboration, no second night of results, and a day-one consensus that no elimination should happen without something checkable. A lone 'detective' claim with a single night-one result is exactly the kind of unfalsifiable assertion this group said it wouldn't act on — Kenji himself committed to that standard in e15. So instead of burning my reveal, I cast the lone pressure vote on Amara to force the accounting round we actually got. It worked: two logged contradictions were surfaced, explained, and resolved. I regret the sequencing — I should have spoken before voting, and I've already owned that. But I did not expect a mafia player to weaponize my hesitation by scripting a counter-claim onto the exact suspicion my vote created.

And that's the tell. Look at the shape of Kenji's claim. It lands at the precise moment the vote record has made me the leading suspicion — Sam said as much in e32, on purely behavioral grounds. A fake detective claim is worth most when it can piggyback on an existing bandwagon, converting soft suspicion into five votes before anyone deliberates. Notice also the rush: 'cast your votes for Noah,' no testing, no questions, and an instruction to the doctor to protect him. A fake claimant who eats the doctor's protection guarantees mafia a safe kill on a real town player tonight. And his framing — 'confirmed mafia, you are caught' — is designed to make questioning the claim feel like scum defense.

His day-one record supports this. One cautious message, a generic threshold commitment, zero information offered. Then, one night later, a fully formed dramatic reveal with a lynch attached. That is not how a careful player behaves; that is how a prepared script behaves.

I can't prove my check to you, and neither can he. So judge us on behavior. My record is consistent: I stated my standard in e18, I've explained my one deviation plainly, and I've held to it since. Kenji's record is a blank followed by an unfalsifiable demand for five votes today.

rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
